title: JESUS SAID, “FOLLOW ME”—NOT “FOLLOW THIS ORGANIZATION”
paragraphs:
JESUS SAID, “FOLLOW ME”—NOT “FOLLOW THIS ORGANIZATION”
What if the thing you have been defending in the name of Jesus has quietly become more important to you than Jesus Himself?
There is a question that can make an entire room uncomfortable.
Not because it attacks Christianity.
Because it exposes how easily Christians can replace Christ with something built around Christ.
If your church disappeared tomorrow, would you still follow Jesus?
If your favorite pastor disappointed you, would you still follow Jesus?
If the ministry that taught you everything suddenly collapsed in scandal, would you still follow Jesus?
If the Christian community where everyone knows your name rejected you…
would Jesus still be enough?
Sit with that.
Because somewhere along the road, a person can become fiercely loyal to a Christian organization while becoming strangely distant from Christ.
You can defend the ministry.
Defend the denomination.
Defend the pastor.
Defend the movement.
Defend the tradition.
Defend the logo.
Defend the people who gave you a spiritual home.
And yet barely recognize the voice of the Shepherd anymore.
That is frightening because Jesus never died so that His people could become trophies belonging to religious personalities.
He died to make sinners His own.
When Jesus walked along the Sea of Galilee and called ordinary fishermen, His invitation was breathtakingly personal.
In the Greek text of Mark 1:17, His summons begins:
“Δεῦτε ὀπίσω μου…”
Deute opisō mou.
“Come after Me.”
There is something almost unsettling about those words.
After Me.
Not after your favorite religious personality.
Not after the person with the largest platform.
Not after whichever Christian tribe makes you feel superior to everybody outside it.
After Me.
Jesus Christ Himself stands at the center.
And we need to understand what this does—and does not—mean.
Jesus saying “Follow Me” is not permission to despise His church.
It is not permission to become spiritually unaccountable.
It is not permission to say, “I don't need other Christians. It's just me and Jesus.”
The New Testament knows nothing of Christianity as permanent spiritual isolation.
Believers gathered.
They prayed together.
They learned together.
They broke bread together.
They served one another.
They submitted to godly leadership.
They corrected one another.
They carried one another's burdens.
Hebrews 10:25 explicitly warns Christians against abandoning their gathering together and instead calls them to encourage one another.
So this message is not:
“Leave the church.”
It is:
Never put the church where only Christ belongs.
There is a difference.
A massive one.
The church belongs to Jesus.
Jesus does not belong to the church.
Your pastor belongs to Jesus.
Jesus does not belong to your pastor.
Your ministry exists for Jesus.
Jesus does not exist to validate your ministry.
Your denomination must bow before Scripture.
Scripture does not bow before your denomination.
And when those lines become blurred, something dangerous begins happening inside sincere people.
We start confusing loyalty to Christ with loyalty to human structures.
The Corinthian church had already begun doing something remarkably familiar.
People were attaching their identities to respected Christian leaders.
Paul.
Apollos.
Cephas.
Listen to the Greek of 1 Corinthians 1:12:
“Ἐγὼ μέν εἰμι Παύλου, Ἐγὼ δὲ Ἀπολλῶ, Ἐγὼ δὲ Κηφᾶ, Ἐγὼ δὲ Χριστοῦ.”
In essence:
“I belong to Paul.”
“I belong to Apollos.”
“I belong to Cephas.”
“I belong to Christ.”
And Paul's response is devastating:
“μεμέρισται ὁ Χριστός;”
Memeristai ho Christos?
“Is Christ divided?”
Then Paul asks the question that destroys personality-centered Christianity:
Was Paul crucified for you?
Were you baptized in Paul's name?
No.
Paul was essentially forcing their eyes away from the servant and back toward the Savior.
Because Paul knew something every Christian leader desperately needs to remember:
Nobody has nail scars in his hands except Jesus.
Your pastor did not carry your sin to Calvary.
Your denomination was not scourged for you.
Your ministry founder did not drink the cup of God's judgment in your place.
Your favorite preacher did not walk out of Joseph's tomb.
Jesus did.
Jesus did.
Jesus did.
And sometimes we need those two words to thunder through everything we have constructed around Christianity until Christ occupies the center again.
Jesus did.
This is why Christian leadership is beautiful when it works correctly.
A faithful pastor does not say, “Look at me.”
He says, “Look at Christ.”
A faithful church does not build cages around believers.
It equips disciples to know Christ, obey Scripture, love one another, proclaim the Gospel, make disciples, pursue holiness, and carry the name of Jesus into the world.
Paul himself could tell believers to imitate him—but notice the boundary:
“Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1).
That final phrase changes everything.
As I am of Christ.
Christian leadership is therefore never absolute.
Jesus is.
Human leaders can help you follow Jesus.
They must never replace Jesus as the object of your faith.
And maybe this is where the article stops being theological and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because perhaps you know what religious disappointment feels like.
Maybe somebody hurt you inside a church.
Maybe someone preached grace from a pulpit and treated people mercilessly behind closed doors.
Maybe you trusted someone because he carried a Bible.
Maybe you believed someone because everyone called him “Pastor.”
Maybe the people who taught you about forgiveness never apologized when they wounded you.
Maybe you watched hypocrisy unfold so badly that eventually you whispered:
“If this is Christianity, I don't want it.”
And perhaps nobody ever told you something you desperately needed to hear:
Jesus Christ is not the hypocrisy committed in His name.
The failure of a Christian does not make Christ a failure.
The corruption of a leader does not corrupt the Gospel.
The collapse of an organization does not collapse the throne of God.
People can misrepresent Jesus.
People can exploit Jesus' name.
People can build empires while preaching about His Kingdom.
People can manipulate Scripture.
People can wound sheep they were supposed to protect.
And Scripture itself repeatedly warns about corrupt shepherds, false teachers, selfish ambition, deception, greed, pride, and spiritual abuse.
So your disappointment may be real.
Your wounds may be deep.
But please…
do not let someone who misrepresented Jesus become the reason you stop looking at Jesus.
Because underneath all the religious noise there is still a Savior calling sinners.
“Follow Me.”
Maybe you haven't heard that invitation clearly in years.
Not:
“Pretend.”
Not:
“Perform.”
Not:
“Make everybody think you're holy.”
Not:
“Become loyal enough to religious people and maybe God will love you.”
Follow Me.
Jesus describes His people in John 10:27 with astonishing intimacy:
“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me.”
Notice the order.
He knows them.
They hear Him.
They follow Him.
Christianity is not ultimately about getting close enough to religious machinery that some holiness rubs off on you.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
And that confrontation goes deeper still.
Because organizations are not the only things capable of replacing Jesus.
Sometimes the organization isn't the idol.
We are.
We want a Jesus who agrees with us.
A Jesus who never confronts our sexual sin.
A Jesus who never touches our greed.
A Jesus who never questions our bitterness.
A Jesus who never challenges our pride.
A Jesus who comforts us but never commands us.
A Jesus who forgives us but never calls us to repentance.
A Jesus who saves us from hell but leaves us comfortably sitting on the throne of our own lives.
But that Jesus does not exist.
The biblical Jesus says:
Follow Me.
Following means He leads.
Following means I don't.
Following means His Word can correct me.
Following means my desires are not automatically holy simply because they are mine.
Following means repentance.
Following means surrender.
Following means grace.
Following means sometimes discovering that the thing I have defended for years was wrong.
And this is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because the Gospel says something devastating about every one of us.
We cannot save ourselves.
Not through church attendance.
Not through denominational membership.
Not through religious knowledge.
Not through Christian merchandise.
Not through volunteering.
Not through theological vocabulary.
Not through knowing famous pastors.
Not even through sharing this article.
Those things cannot purchase salvation.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
We have sinned against a holy God.
And Christianity does not begin with humanity climbing toward God.
It begins with God coming after humanity.
Christ entered our broken world.
The sinless One stood where sinners deserved to stand.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered not as wages for religious achievement but as grace received through faith in Christ.
That changes everything.
You don't follow Jesus so He will finally decide to love you.
You follow because the Savior who loved sinners gave Himself for them.
You don't repent to purchase grace.
Grace brings you to the place where you finally stop defending the sin destroying you.
And maybe your scandal isn't public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you know exactly how to smile at church.
You know when to raise your hands.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You know what verses to post.
You know how to look spiritually alive.
But when the room gets quiet…
you know.
The pornography.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The secret messages.
The addiction.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The double life.
The hatred you keep feeding.
The forgiveness you keep refusing.
The private compromises you would be horrified to see projected onto the church screen.
And somehow you have remained close enough to Christian culture to look alive while becoming increasingly distant from Christ.
Then hear Him again.
Not the organization.
Not this page.
Not me.
Jesus.
Follow Me.
Not when you're cleaned up.
Come to Him so He can cleanse you.
Not when your scandal disappears.
Bring your scandal into the light of His grace.
Not when you've finally become worthy.
You never will.
That is why grace is grace.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop hiding.
Confess your sin to God.
Run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
Because the wonder of Christianity isn't that good people finally found the right religious organization.
The wonder is that guilty people found a crucified and risen Savior.
That is the heartbeat behind everything we mean when we say:
Peter had a scandal.
He denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church was riddled with division and sin.
Yet Jesus kept rewriting human stories through repentance, mercy, restoration, truth, and grace.
That does not mean sin doesn't matter.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace cost blood.
Grace has wounds.
Grace has a cross standing behind it.
The Gospel doesn't say your sin wasn't serious.
The Gospel says your sin was so serious Christ died—and God's mercy is so extraordinary that sinners who repent and believe can be forgiven.
So perhaps the most important question isn't:
“What church are you part of?”
That matters.
Finding a biblically faithful local church matters deeply.
Christian community matters.
Sound doctrine matters.
Godly leadership matters.
Accountability matters.
But there is a question underneath all of those:
Whose voice ultimately owns your allegiance?
When Jesus and your culture disagree, who wins?
When Scripture and your favorite preacher disagree, who wins?
When biblical truth and denominational tradition appear to conflict, which one gets examined?
When following Jesus costs reputation, comfort, relationships, money, opportunities, or applause…
will you still follow?
Because there may come a moment when everyone around you is shouting one direction…
and the Shepherd is calling you another.
Know His voice.
Know His Word.
Know the Gospel.
Love His church without worshiping institutions.
Honor faithful leaders without idolizing personalities.
Receive correction without surrendering biblical discernment.
Serve ministries without confusing the ministry with the Master.
And never give another human being the throne belonging to Jesus Christ.
Be honest before God.
Let believers who see it pray.
And if Christ has already rescued you from religious performance, spiritual abuse, hidden sin, pride, addiction, hypocrisy, or a season when you nearly walked away, tell somebody what Jesus did.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed tonight.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
But if this truth helped you, sharing it can place the Gospel in front of someone we may never reach otherwise.
Someone may have confused a bad experience with Christians for the character of Christ.
Someone may be one disappointment away from abandoning the faith.
Someone may never enter a church building—but they might read the article you were courageous enough to share.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Invite the skeptic.
Even invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to them.
Not as a payment to God.
Not as proof that you love Jesus.
Not as a spiritual transaction.
Follow Jesus.
Find a faithful church that helps you follow Jesus.
Love Christians because you follow Jesus.
Honor faithful pastors because you follow Jesus.
Read Scripture because you want to know Jesus rightly.
Reject false teaching because you belong to Jesus.
Forgive because Jesus forgave you.
Repent because Jesus is Lord.
Serve because Jesus served.
Love because Jesus loved.
Carry your cross because Jesus called you.
And when human heroes fall…
when organizations change…
when denominations disappoint…
when Christian celebrities disappear…
when movements come and go…
when your own strength fails…
there will still be nail-scarred hands.
There will still be an empty tomb.
There will still be a risen King.
There will still be grace for repentant sinners.
And there will still be that voice cutting through all the noise:
“Follow Me.”
Because one day every platform will become irrelevant, every human name will fade from the spotlight, every organization will eventually pass into history…
but the voice that once said “Follow Me” will still be the only voice worth following when everything else is gone.
